item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Eric Lauer and other recent Dodgers regular-season helpers
item.dc:creator: Estevão Maximo
item.description: The success of a dominant team over a lengthy period like the Dodgers' relies on an adaptability to work your way through multiple iterations of a roster. While in the postseason you can find success in different ways, one aspect of regular-season success is how you handle injuries, particularly for a team as cautious as the Dodgers. A common theme in recent seasons has been the Dodgers' pitching staff overcoming all sorts of obstacles to consistently provide terrific numbers. Postseason basebal
item.content:encoded:
The success of a dominant team over a lengthy period like the Dodgers' relies on an adaptability to work your way through multiple iterations of a roster. While in the postseason you can find success in different ways, one aspect of regular-season success is how you handle injuries, particularly for a team as cautious as the Dodgers.
A common theme in recent seasons has been the Dodgers' pitching staff overcoming all sorts of obstacles to consistently provide terrific numbers. Postseason baseball funnels everything, and meritocracy only takes you so far when the goal is to win short series, but that doesn't mean the impact of productive but unceremoniously overlooked starters shouldn't get the credit it rightfully deserves.
There are layers of this tier, and we're not here to discuss the Justin Wrobleskis of the world, who'll morph into a different but still impactful role because their talent level demands a presence on the postseason roster, one way or another. This is an article for the Eric Lauers — pitchers who served a very specific and much-needed purpose in the regular season, but whose eventual playoff showing would only come in garbage-time scenarios; in Lauer's case, not even that, given he has ended the season on the injured list.
When Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow went down this year, as they often do in the regular season, the Dodgers took to the market early in the season for a veteran steady presence. Lauer did more than just go out there with league-average production or so.
The former Brewer worked on some adjustments with the Dodgers' pitching staff and led the team to a win in each of his first nine starts, boasting an ERA under 3.00 through that period. It'd be no stretch to argue that, at the very least, this chase for a playoff bye would look a lot different with a ton more pressure had it not been for Lauer's timely production. His final line with the Dodgers looks far worse than he pitched due to a couple of blowups against NL Central teams (4.50 ERA in 12 games), but his impact through most of that period was undeniable.
Even in the best of moments for Lauer with the Dodgers prior to his season-ending injury, it was evident that he would not play a key role in the playoffs, but it was about doing a specific job. While he was the best example in this year's current squad, going back through the recent track record, the names pile up, and here we'll look at a few others that might stand out—who perhaps didn't receive the right amount of due at the time, and certainly not when playoff ball rolled around.
Prospects with potentially limited big-league upside
This season's starting pitching problems are a cakewalk in comparison with what this team had to deal with a year ago. On the lookout for starting pitching contributions for much of the 2025 campaign, the Dodgers saw Dustin May come full circle on a sped-up version of your traditional career, entering the innings-eater portion far earlier than anyone would've anticipated, one of three starters on the team to cover 100-plus innings, this despite getting dealt at the deadline.
May, more than probably any other pitcher on this list, really pushed the envelope of what we can consider helpful volume, even with the caveat of potential uncertainty on door number two. It's easy to be dismissive of his ERA in the high 4.00s that got progressively worse until the team dealt him when it got healthier in the second half—through the majority of those innings, though, it literally had no one else. And if we want to get a little cute about it, the health he displayed in that period certainly played a role in helping the Dodgers land the offer they sought, with James Tibbs III joining the fold. It's about finding advantages anywhere.
If May represents the low end of the expectation pool for a pitcher of his caliber receiving this type of role in a contending team, a year prior Gavin Stone showed the best-case scenario. On the way to their second World Series of this era, it was the youngster Stone who led the Dodgers in innings pitched that regular season, before injuries cut short his campaign and development, which has been affected until the present day.
Even before the injuries, it was becoming increasingly clear in the second half of that 2024 campaign that Stone's postseason role would diminish, particularly so after the Dodgers acquired Jack Flaherty at the deadline. The changeup-heavy approach with below-average strikeout numbers caused enough concern that he likely wouldn't have stuck in the rotation one way or another.
Both in very different places right now, one still in the organization, May and Stone were once regarded as highly touted pitching prospects. Although their development wasn't as smooth as the Dodgers would've liked, they showed up to provide support at times of need, and their contributions meant a lot in championship-winning seasons.
Former stars in unique spots
Clayton Kershaw gave his best years to the Dodgers when they weren't nearly at their best and did so with the utmost grace and power. After a second chapter of his career, still dominant but maybe not quite Kershaw-dominant, came to an end in 2023, he stuck around for a couple of more years and only then genuinely looked mortal, but still quite helpful.
Missing the bulk of the 2024 season recovering from shoulder surgery, Kershaw came back healthier for one final year in 2025, and while his All-Star nomination might've been a tad sentimental, the 11-2 record was eye-catching, with a productive 124 ERA+.
Sitting below 90 MPH on his heater, there were clear limitations to what Kershaw could provide, but not only did he appear on the postseason roster. But he also managed to get one immense out in the never-ending Game 3 of that year's World Series. The plan was never to have him play a big role in October, but circumstances gave him a memorable cameo.
Going back to the regular season contributions, Kershaw, alongside May, was one of three Dodgers starters to surpass 100 innings in 2025. On the subject of his impact on that 93-69 record, there was nothing sentimental about it; he thoroughly helped a team that relied on him far more than expected.
Going back a few more years, the Dodgers needed to take on the David Price contract in order for the Mookie Betts deal to go through with Boston. And although that was a bad deal, it didn't mean Price couldn't be of assistance.
Opting out of the 2020 campaign, Price came in 2021 ready to embrace whatever role the Dodgers had for him, and he delivered a 105 ERA+ in over 70 innings, moving back and forth between the rotation and the bullpen. While the rotation was healthier that year, it didn't mean his presence went unnoticed, one of the more heavily used arms navigating between the rotation and the bullpen.
The OGs of this role in this run
When you first started reading this article, there is a decent chance one of the first names that came to mind was Mitch White or, particularly, Ross Stripling — the latter personally thanked by Dave Roberts in the World Series-winning speech back in 2020, a year in which he was traded from the team that August.
Between 2016 and 2019, Stripling pitched nearly 400 innings of regular-season baseball with a 115 ERA+, moving around to whatever role fit the team best. Seeing them finally break through to win it all the year in which he was dealt (2020) quickly made Dave and many others remember all he had done for this team.
It's a shame that at his best in 2018, working primarily as a starter, Stripling saw his campaign cut short due to injury and couldn't be available in that postseason. In 2020, the Dodgers stuck with him as much as possible, but eventually cutting ties seemed like the only answer with an ERA well above 5.00 in a shortened campaign.
White is the ideal example to note how, in most of these cases, whether the Dodgers get these players late, early, or even develop them from the minors, they seem to shine brightest here. In three seasons with the Dodgers, White had a 116 ERA+ in a little over 100 innings. Not only did he fail to reach similar heights after leaving the team, but his exposure was very limited, covering just 79.1 innings in two seasons since. Out of the bigs since 2024.
Surely there were other names in recent memory that we might've skipped over. Let us know who your favorite regular-season starting pitcher contributor is, or even all-time. It's always a fun conversation to have with no right or wrong answer.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts had some high praise for right-handed pitcher Emmet Sheehan after his last start, hinting at the strong possibility of him making the team's postseason roster.
Sheehan, who was recently optioned back to Triple-A Oklahoma City, seems like a lock to join the team for the National League Division Series next weekend.
“I’ve loved the version we’ve seen of Emmet the last three outings,” Roberts said. “He’s been fantastic.
“We’ve seen confidence. We’ve seen when you’re essentially fighting for your life to create an opportunity for yourself. That’s what I see. There’s urgency. I like the way that he’s trusting his stuff. He’s in a good spot physically, and you know the performance has been fantastic.”
The 26-year-old pitcher was masterful in his final outing of the regular season on Sunday in the Dodgers' win over the San Francisco Giants, pitching 5.1 shutout innings and striking out nine batters. He entered in the second inning after Jack Dreyer pitched the first, giving him more experience coming out of the bullpen.
Overall, Sheehan has looked incredible in his three September outings. He's allowed just one run over 17 innings with 24 strikeouts.
“I think that obviously there’s a 97 [mph] that plays better, but 94-95 commanded still misses bats,” Roberts said of Sheehan. “That’s one part of it. The other part of it is holding the velocity. And so, for me, the last three or four since he’s been back here, he’s held those 94s and 95s for the, call it, 85 pitches.”
This season, Sheehan owns a 5-8 record with a 4.57 ERA, 1.18 WHIP and 132 strikeouts in 112.1 innings across 23 appearances.
Sheehan is expected to be in the Dodgers' bullpen for this year's postseason, just as he was last year.
During the 2025 postseason, Sheehan made six relief appearances, posting an 8.59 ERA and recording six strikeouts over 7.1 innings. However, he said he's more prepared this time around, and expects to have better results in his now more familiar role.
“Definitely,” Sheehan said. “I think the routine of everything can be a little bit hard to adjust to right away. So having that experience helps a lot. Just getting back into that, I know what I need to do to get ready to go into the game.”
Sheehan will give the Dodgers a multi-inning option out of the bullpen. If he's pitching like he has over the last few weeks, he could be a serious weapon for LA.

item.content:encoded:
The AL and NL Wild Card Series presented by AbbVie begins Tuesday, Sept. 29 with many of MLB’s most popular players preparing to take center stage. Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers, Aaron Judge of the New York Yankees and Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs are leading the league in most popular player jerseys as their respective Clubs enter the final weekend of the regular season with Postseason berths secured.
Ohtani’s popularity reached new heights as he became the first player to finish four straight seasons with the most popular player jersey in the Majors since tracking began in 2010. Since 2023, fans have purchased Ohtani’s Nike jersey more than any other in the U.S., Japan and worldwide. With Dodgers teammate and reigning Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s jersey ranking no. 9 and Chicago White Sox All-Star slugger Munetaka Murakami debuting on the list at no. 20, this is also the first season that three MLB Players from Japan have their jerseys in the top 20.
After becoming only the seventh player in MLB history and first Cubs player to hit at least 40 home runs and steal at least 40 bases in a single season, Crow-Armstrong’s jersey finished as the third most popular of the season – the highest ranking for a Cubs star since Javier Báez finished third in 2018.
This list, released jointly today by MLB and MLB Players, Inc. (MLBPI), accounts for sales of Nike jerseys from the Fanatics network of sites, including MLBShop.com, since Opening Day of the 2026 Championship Season.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers news: LA set to receive huge Dalton Rushing boost right before playoffs appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
With the Los Angeles Dodgers preparing for the upcoming 2026 MLB Playoffs, the team is looking to get back key players from injuries, with catcher Dalton Rushing about to return to the roster. As the Dodgers look to finalize their playoff strategy ahead of the postseason, the team gets huge news regarding the 25-year-old catcher.
According to MLB.com, Rushing is "set to be activated" from the 10-day injured list for the final regular-season series against the San Francisco Giants. Rushing last played for Los Angeles Sept. 4, as the star had been dealing with "right elbow discomfort," though it goes beyond that, as he'll only be a hitter this season after a "partial tear of the ulnar collateral ligament in his right elbow.
Rushing will have three games to prove his worth on the Dodgers' postseason roster, but there's no denying that Los Angeles manager Dave Roberts wants to give him a shot.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"Just the circumstances of his situation, it's just tough to just be hurt, be back, then be hurt again," Roberts said Thursday, via Sonja Chen of MLB.com. "And then take three pinch-hit at-bats, potentially, and then say, 'Hey, you're on the roster.' What he's done for us this season certainly deserves some consideration. That's kind of giving him the respect and thoughtfulness of what he's done for us."
More on the decision regarding Dodgers' Dalton Rushing
With three games left in the regular season for the Dodgers, Rushing has recorded a .249 batting average to go along with 12 home runs and 36 RBIs in 78 games and 221 plate appearances. While the small sample size of three games could be discouraging for his chances at making Los Angeles' playoff roster, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman is also looking at his season as a whole.
"He's done everything he can to put himself in a position to be in the conversation for us as we're making our postseason roster," Friedman said.
At any rate, it remains to be seen how Rushing plays after returning from the injured list with an elbow issue as Friday starts the series against the Giants.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers fans have spoken, and they want rookie Josue De Paula back with the team to provide a spark.
Why the Dodgers Demoted De Paula
After 11 stellar games, in which De Paula looked amazing at the plate, the Dodgers demoted him on Wednesday, September 23rd, sending him back to the minors.
With Shohei Ohtani returning from the injured list, he would assume the designated hitter role from De Paula. Additionally, Dalton Rushing is returning to get some at-bats and make his case for a postseason roster spot.
De Paula was hitting .323/.500/.545 with a 1.081 OPS, making pitchers work and bringing a youthful edge to an older roster.
After his demotion, manager Dave Roberts and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman both praised De Paula and made it clear he will be considered for a spot on the postseason roster.
Since he was demoted on Wednesday and players must wait 10 days to be promoted back to the major leagues, he would be in line to return in time for Game 1 of the NLDS.
While the decision-makers are giving Rushing a chance to make his case and weigh their options, Dodgers Nation has already decided.
Dodgers Fans Demand De Paula
Following his demotion, the Dodgers have scored just two runs over the last 18 innings, losing both games to the San Diego Padres.
In his last game on Tuesday, September 22nd, De Paula went 2-for-3 with a triple, a walk, and a stolen base.
With the two-game cold stretch since his absence, fans want him back in the mix.
“Hmm, maybe sending JDP down wasn’t the right move after all,” a fan said after the Dodgers lost on Thursday.
“Miss you JDP,” another commented.
“Damn JDP and will smith really carry that much weight huh,” a third added.
“Josue was only gonna get better BRING HIM BACK,” a fourth wrote.
As for the postseason, fans don’t even think it’s a question of whether De Paula should be on the team.
“Dude was on fire!! And confident!! Don’t understand at all!! And he was starting and succeeding,” a fan said.
“JDP needs to be there. He proved it!!” another chimed in.
“Cmon guys, we all know JDP will make that playoff roster, if he doesn’t I’m going to the front office myself,” a third fan said.
Safe to say, the outrage if De Paula is not on the postseason roster will be palpable.

item.title: [sportingnews.com] Yankees' Cam Schlittler joins Sandy Koufax in MLB history that should end AL Cy Young debate | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan
item.description: The New York Yankees might not have won the AL East, but they've clinched a home playoff series against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round. This Yankees team might not have Aaron Judge when the playoffs begin, but the presence of Cam Schlittler and the rest of the rotation should give Yankees fans a lot of confidence this October. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees might not have won the AL East, but they've clinched a home playoff series against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round.
This Yankees team might not have Aaron Judge when the playoffs begin, but the presence of Cam Schlittler and the rest of the rotation should give Yankees fans a lot of confidence this October.
Speaking of Schlittler, his bid to win the AL Cy Young should be cemented after his last start of the year. According to ESPN Insights, Schlittler's start made some MLB history, joining Sandy Koufax and Grover Alexander in an incredible feat that should end the Cy Young race in the AL, if it wasn't over already.
Cam Schlittler makes MLB history with 25th strong outing
"This was Cam Schlittler's 25th start this season with 1 or 0 ER allowed," ESPN Insights shared. "That ties Sandy Koufax and Grover Alexander for the 2nd-most starts with 1 or 0 ER in a season since 1913, excluding openers."
Schlittler has been in the race for the AL Cy Young all season, and while Dylan Cease of the Toronto Blue Jays and Parker Messick of the Cleveland Guardians both had solid cases, neither can really compare to Schlittler now.
After this history-tying start from Schlittler, which joins him with two legends in MLB history with the most starts allowing at most one run in a season, his bid for the AL Cy Young should be cemented.
While he only went three innings to reach his 25th start allowing no more than one run, it's still a noteworthy accomplishment for Schlittler.
Schlittler finishes his 2026, likely Cy Young-winning season, with a 1.96 ERA, 239 strikeouts, a 14-6 record, a 0.92 WHIP, and only 49 walks allowed in 193.2 innings in 33 starts.
He should be the unquestioned AL Cy Young winner, and this feat, tying Koufax and Alexander with the second-most starts in a season allowing no more than one run, should solidify his status as the AL's best pitcher this season.

item.title: [UNANIMO Deportes] Fernando Valenzuela: cómo la "Fernandomanía" transformó a la MLB - UNANIMO Deportes
item.dc:creator: Unanimo Deportes
item.description: Con su peculiar estilo al lanzar y mirar al cielo, Fernando Valenzuela cautivó a la Major League Baseball (MLB), desató la famosa “Fernandomanía” y se convirtió en una de las leyendas hispanas en la historia del deporte a la cual se le rinde tributo en el Mes de la Herencia Hispana. - LEER MÁS SOBRE: Oficializan el Día de Fernando Valenzuela, ¿cuándo es?} - LEER MÁS SOBRE: Fernando Valenzuela recibe otro chance para entrar al Salón de la Fama - LEER MÁS SOBRE: VIDEO: Mexicanos que han ganado una
item.content:encoded:
Con su peculiar estilo al lanzar y mirar al cielo, Fernando Valenzuela cautivó a la Major League Baseball (MLB), desató la famosa “Fernandomanía” y se convirtió en una de las leyendas hispanas en la historia del deporte a la cual se le rinde tributo en el Mes de la Herencia Hispana.
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: Oficializan el Día de Fernando Valenzuela, ¿cuándo es?}
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: Fernando Valenzuela recibe otro chance para entrar al Salón de la Fama
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: VIDEO: Mexicanos que han ganado una Serie Mundial de MLB
El llamado “Toro” Valenzuela, quien nació el 1 de noviembre de 1960, en Etchohuaquila, municipio de Navojoa, Sonora, México, fue firmado por Los Angeles Dodgers en julio del 1979, y un año después debutó en las Mayores cerca de concluir la temporada dejando una grata impresión sobre su accionar al conseguir marca de 2-0 y un rescate en 10 juegos.
Sin embargo, nadie imaginó lo que sucedería dos años más tarde con ese lanzador regordete.
Suscríbete al Newsletter de Unanimo y recibe gratis las últimas noticias. Dale click aquí
Aunque Jerry Reuss estaba contemplado para iniciar el Día Inaugural, el zurdo se lastimó una pierna un día antes y Tom LaSorda, manager de los Dodgers, sorprendió al darle la apertura al novato mexicano de 20 años para enfrentar a los Houston Astros.
Con un aplomo increíble y nervios de acero, Valenzuela respondió con una joya monticular al blanquear al equipo tejano por 2-0 cediendo apenas cinco hits y dos bases por bolas. Ahí fue que comenzó la llamada “Fernandomanía”.
En sus primeras ocho aperturas, el sonorense tuvo récord de 8-0, con siete juegos completos, incluyendo cinco blanqueadas y cedió apenas cuatro carreras limpias en 72 entradas, convirtiéndose en toda una celebridad en Los Ángeles, particularmente entre la población mexicana de la ciudad, además de acaparar los titulares del béisbol alrededor de la nación.
Todos hablaban del pitcher mexicano que parecía tener mucho más que 20 años y que cuando lanzaba miraba al cielo justo antes de soltar la pelota hacia el plato.
“Estaba emocionado”, recordó Valenzuela en el libro “Hermanos en Brazos: Koufax, Kershaw y la extraordinaria tradición de lanzadores de los Dodgers” escrito por Jon Weisman. “Fue bueno, pero difícil al mismo tiempo”.
“En el terreno, estaba bien. Fuera del terreno, después de los juegos, a veces la gente o los medios no entendían, querían la entrevista de inmediato, y yo tenía que trabajar, tenía que estar con el equipo. En ese tiempo, esa fue la parte difícil, pero cuando salía al campo, fue emocionante, porque sabía lo que tenía que hacer. Tenía mucha confianza en mi repertorio”.
Valenzuela terminó la temporada, que se vio paralizada entre el 12 de junio al 31 de julio debido a una huelga de jugadores, con marca de 13-7 y un promedio de carreras limpias de 2.48, y fue líder de ponches (180), juegos completos (11), blanqueadas (8) y entradas lanzadas (192.1). También tuvo récord de 3-1 en la postemporada que vio a los Dodgers coronarse como campeón de la Serie Mundial.
Su actuación fue tan espectacular que ganó el premio de Novato del Año y se convirtió en el único novato en ganar un premio Cy Young.
Apoyados en su famoso lanzamiento de screwball o tirabuzón, de “El Toro de Etchohuaquila” consiguió 141 victorias con 116 derrotas en su carrera de 11 años con los Dodgers (1980-1990). Fue nombrado al Juego de Estrellas en seis ocasiones, ganó 20 juegos o más en una temporada (1986) y el 29 de junio del 1990 lanzó un no-hitter contra los St. Louis Cardinals, terminando la campaña con 13-13 y una efectividad de 4.59 en 33 aperturas.
La era de Valenzuela en Los Angeles llegó a su fin cuando el equipo lo dejó libre luego de un discreto entrenamiento primaveral en 1991. Ahí comenzó un periodo de inestabilidad en su carrera al pasar por seis organizaciones (California, Detroit -entrenamiento primaveral-, Baltimore, Philadelphia, San Diego, St. Louis) y algunas estancias en el béisbol mexicano.
Su mejor temporada fue en el 1996 con los San Diego Padres con los cuales logró récord de 13–8 y una efectividad de 3.62. Un año después se retiró como miembro de los Cardenales, concluyendo su carrera en las Grandes Ligas con marca de 173–153 y 3.54 de ERA, aunque años después retornó al béisbol mexicano.
Sin embargo, Valenzuela, siempre es recordado con cariño y nostalgia por sus hazañas con los Dodgers y la “Fernandomanía”. Desde que terminó sus días con la organización ningún otro jugador ha vestido su número 34 por respeto al famoso “Toro”.
En sus ultimo días fue hospitalizado debido a una enfermedad hepática que acabó desencadenando un colapso multiorgánico.
El médico a cargo de su autopsia sospecha que pudo haber padecido la enfermedad de Creutzfeldt-Jakob, un raro y grave trastorno cerebral que afecta la función mental y el movimiento. Esta enfermedad, es causada por proteínas anormales en el cerebro llamadas priones, las cuales provocan un rápido deterioro neurológico que lleva a síntomas graves como demencia, pérdida de coordinación y, en última instancia, la muerte.
El Ayuntamiento de Los Ángeles decidió instituir, el 1 de noviembre —fecha de su natalicio— como el “Día de Fernando Valenzuela”, esto a manera de reconocimiento especial en su memoria destacando no sólo los logros deportivos del lanzador, sino también el impacto cultural que tuvo en la comunidad latina y en la identidad de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles. Su influencia trascendió los estadios y se convirtió en un puente entre generaciones de aficionados.
A pesar de su trayectoria en la Gran Carpa, Valenzuela no ha logrado obtener la votación necesaria para asegurar su ingreso al Salón de la Fama de Cooperstown.
El comité evaluador, compuesto por 16 miembros, tiende a priorizar las estadísticas acumuladas y métricas tradicionales de los lanzadores de tal manera que los números del mexicano no resultan suficientes para inmortalizarlo, al menos todavía.
Tabla de posiciones de la MLBConsulta las posiciones y los resultados actualizados.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Glasnow Feeling a Rhythm as Dodgers Head into Postseason
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Tyler Glasnow may not have gotten the result he wanted in Thursday night’s 4-1 loss to the Padres, but the Dodgers right-hander came away from his final regular-season start feeling particularly encouraged about his preparation for October. Glasnow held San Diego hitless through five innings before running into trouble in the sixth and seventh. He finished with 11 strikeouts over 6 1/3 innings, allowing three hits and three earned runs. More importantly, he believes he has foun
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Tyler Glasnow may not have gotten the result he wanted in Thursday night’s 4-1 loss to the Padres, but the Dodgers right-hander came away from his final regular-season start feeling particularly encouraged about his preparation for October.
Glasnow held San Diego hitless through five innings before running into trouble in the sixth and seventh. He finished with 11 strikeouts over 6 1/3 innings, allowing three hits and three earned runs. More importantly, he believes he has found the rhythm and timing that had occasionally eluded him since returning from the injured list.
“Good. I felt good the whole game,” Glasnow said afterward. “I think my timing was good today. Felt really good in the quick step.”
Asked about the effectiveness of his fastball and curveball combination, Glasnow credited the way the two pitches worked together to keep San Diego’s hitters off balance.
“I think it was tunneling pretty well,” he explained. “I think the two-seamer was good, but I leaned on the heater-curveball combo today a lot.”
An Important Adjustment With Runners Aboard
One of Glasnow’s biggest takeaways from Thursday’s outing had little to do with his 11 strikeouts. Instead, he was particularly pleased with the progress he made pitching from the stretch and controlling the running game.
“I’m glad I kind of figured out that quick step with guys on,” Glasnow said. “I think just the running game has always been kind of rough for me this year, and I think today, even with Tati stealing, I just think I was a bit quicker and timing felt a lot better in that quick step.”
“I’m just happy to take that into my next step.”
Glasnow acknowledged that his last couple of starts have been especially encouraging as he prepares for his next assignment, which will come in the postseason.
“The last couple have been a lot better for me timing-wise,” he said. “I feel like I’m in a pretty good rhythm right now, so it’s the perfect time to bring it into the postseason.”
Asked whether Thursday’s outing was a good one to carry into an extended layoff, Glasnow pointed to his recent performances and his physical condition.
“I think each start is kind of its own thing, but it is encouraging to feel good these last two and just feel strong and healthy. I can take that into the postseason for sure.”
First-Round Bye Offers Some Comfort, but No Guarantees
With the Dodgers having secured the National League’s second seed and a first-round bye thanks to Atlanta’s loss earlier Thursday, Glasnow was asked how much of an advantage the extra rest might provide.
He wasn’t particularly interested in assigning too much importance to the team’s postseason path.
“We’ve had byes in previous years and not done well. We’ve been wild cards and all,” Glasnow said. “I think it’s just all random. It’s a bit comforting, I guess, to have a bye, but I think any situation we’re in, we’re going to play well.”
As for the possibility of facing the Padres again in October, Glasnow dismissed the idea that Thursday’s result would necessarily carry over into a future matchup.
“I think each start is its own thing,” he said. “Like I said, I’m just happy timing and everything feel good, and I think anything going forward is just kind of a new day.”
A Message to Dodger Fans
Glasnow closed his interview with a brief message for the Dodger Stadium faithful, who will next see him on the mound in a postseason game.
“Thanks for supporting us. Come out and be loud, and we’re all looking forward to it.”
For the Dodgers, Thursday’s loss was disappointing, but Glasnow’s performance provided another encouraging indication that their starting rotation is coming together at the right time. With his health intact, his timing improving and his fastball-curveball combination working effectively, the right-hander appears ready for the challenge ahead.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Dodgers manager shares opinion on Petco Park, Padres' postseason berths
item.dc:creator: Matt Borelli
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres just faced each other for the final time during the regular season up against a backdrop of both teams having October on their minds. The Dodgers are heading back to the playoffs for the 14th consecutive season and clinched the National League West title for a fifth year in a row. That since has been followed by securing a first-round bye in the playoffs. Meanwhile, the Padres punched their ticket for the playoffs by defeating the Dodgers on Thursday
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres just faced each other for the final time during the regular season up against a backdrop of both teams having October on their minds.
The Dodgers are heading back to the playoffs for the 14th consecutive season and clinched the National League West title for a fifth year in a row. That since has been followed by securing a first-round bye in the playoffs.
Meanwhile, the Padres punched their ticket for the playoffs by defeating the Dodgers on Thursday night. The Padres are in the postseason for a franchise-record third consecutive season, and their fifth appearance in the last seven years.
“Small market, huh?” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts jokingly asked. “I think they’ve certainly accrued a lot of talent, the fanbase is very supportive, Petco is one of the best places to play a ballgame and take in a baseball game.
“I think (Craig) Stammen is great and I like what they’ve done. I think they’ve done some good things. A.J. (Preller) has done a great job. They’re always a thorn in our side and great competition.”
The Padres are often championed for their willingness to put a competitive product on the field each season despite playing in a small market. Their resurgence began under former owner Peter Seidler and is now continuing with José E. Feliciano at the helm.
The Padres haven’t been able to get over the hump to this point, but they hope that changes this year.
Under the current NL postseason bracket, San Diego would have to get past the Wild Card Series and Division Series for a potential showdown with the Dodgers in the Championship Series. The teams have met three times in MLB postseason history — all since 2020 — with L.A. winning two of those series.
Dave Roberts: Padres ‘good’ test for Dodgers
Prior to their three-game series beginning at Dodger Stadium, Roberts said the Padres being in town would present a good tuneup for the Dodgers before they head into the postseason.
“I think it’s going to be a good kind of primer,” Roberts said. “They’re a very talented team, they’re playing as good as anyone in all of baseball. I’m looking forward to playing those guys and just kind of ramping it up a little bit more for our guys.”

item.title: [FanSided] Why MLB fans should root for Roki Sasaki in the playoffs, not revel in Dodgers downfall
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: Crossing the Pacific Ocean and signing with the Los Angeles Dodgers meant cultural and personal transitions for prized Japanese import Roki Sasaki. But when Sasaki officially met the U.S. media in early 2025, he made it clear he and his newest fanbase had two things in common: baseball and grief. item.content:encoded:
Crossing the Pacific Ocean and signing with the Los Angeles Dodgers meant cultural and personal transitions for prized Japanese import Roki Sasaki.
But when Sasaki officially met the U.S. media in early 2025, he made it clear he and his newest fanbase had two things in common: baseball and grief.
Sasaki returned from the injured list this week just as a March 2025 story by the Dodgers’ official website resurfaced on social media. At the time, California was still recovering from the January 2025 wildfires that ravaged the Los Angeles area, an unfortunately familiar sight for their newest pitcher.
Nearly 15 years earlier, Sasaki lost his father, grandparents, and his family’s home in the March 2011 tsunami. He turned to baseball as an escape, just as so many others affected by tragedy often do.
"Los Angeles is facing challenging and difficult times right now,” Sasaki said in January 2025, “and as a member of the Dodgers, starting today, I am dedicated to give my best and strive forward together with the people of the city."
Baseball fans can support Roki Sasaki without rooting for the Los Angeles Dodgers
This might sound contradictory, but hear us out.
We just saw Mets fans overwhelmingly cheer for Pete Alonso, even after he smashed a game-tying home run. Citi Field cared far more about Alonso the player than it did the Orioles as a team. Had the Orioles somehow snuck into the postseason, we imagine there’d be plenty of Mets fans with even the slightest rooting interest.
The same principle — or, at least, an extremely similar one — easily applies to Sasaki. Forget the fact he signed with the reigning World Series champions and played a pivotal role during last year’s title run. He’s still a human being with emotions who went through a horrifically traumatic experience; nearly 20,000 people are believed to have died in the Great East Japan Earthquake, and over 2,550 people remained missing as of 2021.
And above all else, Sasaki hasn’t done anything wrong beyond struggling to hit the strike zone. But compare that to some of the other notable names we’ll see this postseason. San Diego’s Fernando Tatis Jr. and Ramón Laureano each served PED-related suspensions. Boston’s Jarren Duran has feuded with fans and media in a way Red Sox Nation eventually stopped defending.
We’ve long been critical of both Sasaki and how the Dodgers have refused to make him a full-time reliever. Dave Roberts confirmed earlier this week the 24-year-old will pitch out of the bullpen during the postseason, just as he did last October, and the first impressions were positive; Sasaki threw a scoreless inning and didn’t allow a walk against the Padres on Tuesday night.
We wouldn’t blame you for hoping the Dodgers lose in the NLDS. They’re a superteam seeking their third consecutive championship and fourth in six years. At least three players on the active roster — Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, and Mookie Betts — are widely considered locks for the Hall of Fame, and Tarik Skubal is well on his way.
But when Sasaki comes in from the bullpen, try not to be overly hard on him. Save your vitriol for the umpires and broadcasters.

item.content:encoded:
Mookie Betts batted second against the San Diego Padres on Thursday. The Los Angeles Dodgers returned Shohei Ohtani to his usual leadoff spot.
He played behind Betts on Wednesday at No. 2.
But the change didn’t see success. San Diego beat the Dodgers 4-2 on Thursday night. The win clinched the Padres’ franchise-record third consecutive postseason berth, their fifth in seven seasons.
The Dodgers also secured a bye into the Division Series, avoiding the wild-card round.
Los Angeles now turns to the San Francisco Giants to close the regular season. The three-game series opens Friday at Oracle Park and runs through Sunday. The Dodgers open the postseason on Oct. 3.
Betts went 3-for-4 with a double in Thursday’s loss. He scored a run and drew a walk. He is heating up at the perfect time. In September, his average improved to .367 from .257, with an OPS of 1.177.
Keeping up with the success on the field, Betts also announced major news off the field.
Mookie Betts Announces Major Career News
Betts signed with 3 Arts Sports and Sanders Sports & Entertainment for personal representation.
“We’re excited to announce that 3 Arts Sports and Sanders Sports & Entertainment are joining forces to represent Los Angeles Dodgers star Mookie Betts across brand partnerships, business opportunities and off-field ventures,” the two firms wrote. “Proud to be on Mookie’s team and excited for what’s ahead.”
Betts reshared the post on his own Instagram account.
The two firms will co-manage his personal endorsements, brand partnerships and business development.
3 Arts Sports also represents Travis Kelce, WNBA star Sophie Cunningham and NFL stars Jayden Daniels and Myles Garrett.
Kelce recently signed on as Tommy Hilfiger’s global brand ambassador, a multi-season deal that includes a co-designed menswear collection as a partner of 3 Arts Sports.
Betts face value sits alongside the biggest in the industry.
Shohei Ohtani is Looking Great Ahead of Postseason
Manager Dave Roberts assessed Ohtani after Wednesday’s return. He called Ohtani considerably better than before the injured list stint, roughly an 8 or 9 out of 10 compared with a 5 beforehand.
“The last 2 nights, he’s looked great,” Roberts said. “Really exciting, just missed a homer.”
Ohtani will not pitch in the postseason. The Dodgers shut him down from pitching for the rest of 2026 earlier this month. Roberts said the move lets Ohtani focus fully on hitting.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Tommy Edman Reveals Dodgers' 'Hungry' October Mindset
item.dc:creator: Cameron Kiszla
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers utility player Tommy Edman is gearing up for a run at a third straight championship, and he sat down with Dodgers Nation’s Noel Sanchez to talk about his love for LA and where the team is ahead of the playoffs. Edman, who’s helping give away $25,000 worth of gasoline, has only been in LA for about two and a half years, but he said he feels the SoCal love. “It seems like it was just yesterday, but obviously there’s been a ton that’s happened in those two years,” he said. “I’ve
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers utility player Tommy Edman is gearing up for a run at a third straight championship, and he sat down with Dodgers Nation’s Noel Sanchez to talk about his love for LA and where the team is ahead of the playoffs.
Edman, who’s helping give away $25,000 worth of gasoline, has only been in LA for about two and a half years, but he said he feels the SoCal love.
“It seems like it was just yesterday, but obviously there’s been a ton that’s happened in those two years,” he said. “I’ve really grown to love L.A. The city of L.A. has really embraced me as one of their own. And it’s been nice to come back to SoCal, being from San Diego as well, close to home, so it just feels like a very familiar place to be.”
Getting ready for another tough October
Edman and the Dodgers, having won back-to-back titles, have played more games than anyone else since the start of 2024.
Add into that the 162-game regular season that all teams play and these Dodgers have every reason to be tired.
That said, Edman believes this team still has plenty of gas in the tank to take a run at another World Series title.
“Obviously we’ve gone as far as we can go the last two years,” he said. “So it’s a lot of baseball, but this is what we all play for. All the regular season games kind of lead up to the postseason, and we’re just really excited to get going. You feel that extra adrenaline once you get to postseason, too. It gives us that little boost of energy.”
Dodgers ‘hungrier’ for third championship than the first two
It would be easy to assume that the Dodgers might rest on their laurels.
After all, back-to-back World Series titles is an incredible achievement on its own, but Edman said it only makes the team more driven to win a third.
“I think having experienced the last two Octobers and just how exciting it is actually makes us hungrier for that third World Series title,” he said. “Obviously it’s a lot of baseball to play, but I think it’s just, there’s just nothing that can top it, nothing that can top those crazy October games. So we’re really excited to get going. Obviously, we’ve got to take care of a little bit of business still here in September, but it’s going to be another fun month.”
Do you think the Dodgers will come out hungrier in October?

item.title: [heavy.com] Dodgers Get Encouraging Edwin Diaz News Ahead of MLB Playoffs

In the ninth inning, something encouraging happened. Edwin Diaz took the mound and shut the door. The right-hander struck out two batters and allowed no hits in a clean ninth. After the game, manager Dave Roberts offered a notable assessment of where Diaz stands heading into October. Roberts on Diaz’s Recent Run Roberts has
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers dropped the rubber match of their series against the San Diego Padres on Thursday, falling 4-2 in their regular season home finale at Dodger Stadium.
In the ninth inning, something encouraging happened. Edwin Diaz took the mound and shut the door.
The right-hander struck out two batters and allowed no hits in a clean ninth. After the game, manager Dave Roberts offered a notable assessment of where Diaz stands heading into October.
Roberts on Diaz’s Recent Run
Roberts has watched Diaz closely since returning from the injured list. Each outing has looked better than the last.
“This has been the best of the 4,” Roberts said of Diaz’s performance. “He’ll pitch 1 of the games this weekend, 7th, 8th or 9th.”
Diaz kept it simple when asked what has been working.
“I was throwing strikes,” Diaz said. “That’s my goal.”
The Road Back for Diaz
Diaz’s 2026 season nearly ended before it began. He underwent surgery in late April to remove loose bodies from his right elbow, an injury that put him on the 60-day injured list and cast doubt on whether he would pitch again this year.
His early-season numbers before the surgery were ugly. But the version of Diaz that has returned looks far closer to the pitcher who posted a 1.63 ERA with a 0.87 WHIP for the New York Mets in 2025, ranking second among qualified relievers with a 38 percent strikeout rate.
The Dodgers signed Diaz knowing his ceiling. Getting that ceiling back in September, right before October, changes the complexion of their bullpen.
Final Word for the Dodgers
Edwin Diaz came to Los Angeles to close games in October. Elbow surgery and a lost summer threatened to erase that plan entirely.
Now, the plan is back. Roberts is giving him the ball in the seventh, eighth, or ninth. The strikeouts are coming. The strikes are landing.
The Dodgers’ postseason is approaching. Diaz intends to be a factor. Based on what Roberts said Thursday, the Dodgers believe him.

item.dc:creator: Mark Chiarelli

item.content:encoded:
The Josue De Paula Predicament
Plus: Astros rookie homers three times amid pursuit for AL West crown
Josue De Paula, OF, Dodgers: De Paula already has a major league hit, but in a weird quirk, he hadn’t recorded one in Triple-A entering Thursday’s deciding game of the Pacific Coast League Championship Series. De Paula checked that off early, lining a single to right field in the third inning. He followed with an RBI double later in the game to extend Oklahoma City’s lead to 5-0. Overall, he finished 2-for-5 with a run and an RBI as Oklahoma City won the Pacific Coast League championship.
De Paula started the season in Double-A, hitting .303/.401/.547 with 27 home runs in 124 games. He jumped straight to the majors after Shohei Ohtani got hurt and hit .323/.500/.581 with five extra-base hits, 11 walks and only five strikeouts in 42 plate appearances. Even after that dominant start, De Paula was optioned to Triple-A when Ohtani returned.
In 11 major league games, De Paula played only six innings in the field, spending most of his time at designated hitter. His defense is a major question mark right now, to the extent that the Dodgers don’t seem to trust him in the field. He still could make the Dodgers’ playoff roster because of his upside at the plate in a pinch-hitting role, but it will be difficult for him to carve out a major role this season as long as Ohtani is healthy.
Lucas Spence, OF, Astros: One of the heroes of the Astros’ victory on Thursday that kept them deadlocked with the Rangers atop the American League West was their 23-year-old outfielder. Spence, the No. 9 prospect in the Astros’ system, hit his first three career home runs, powering the Astros to a 7-5 victory.
Spence gave the Astros their first lead with a three-run home run in the second. He then hit the go-ahead home run in the seventh before homering again in the ninth to extend the Astros’ lead to two, which proved to be the final margin.
Spence is now hitting .205/.286/.432 in his first 16 major league games. He was identified as a potential breakout player in the preseason and has seen his stock rise slightly in the Astros’ system after hitting .238/.348/.426 with 13 home runs in 99 games across three levels.
Mike Sirota, OF, Dodgers: Sirota continued his impressive season, reaching base four times in Oklahoma City’s victory to clinch the Pacific Coast League championship. Sirota finished 1-for-2 with three walks, an RBI and a stolen base. He grounded out in the second inning before driving in a run with a single to left in the third to extend Oklahoma City’s lead to 2-0. He then walked in the fifth, seventh and ninth innings.
Sirota finished the series 3-for-11 with three singles and four walks. He hit .307/.461/.526 in 108 games during the regular season and established himself as one of the top outfield prospects in the Dodgers’ system and all of minor league baseball.
Luis Peña, SS, Brewers: Peña, the No. 21 prospect in baseball, underwent surgery on Thursday to repair a fractured left fibula, according to MLB.com's Adam McCalvy. Peña injured his ankle while stealing a base in a game on Sept. 5 and was carted off the field. The 19-year-old was limited to just 70 games in 2026 and spent the bulk of the year with High-A Wisconsin. He hit .296/.380/.415 with 35 stolen bases across three stops.
Peña also missed nearly a month early in the season after passing out in the dugout during a game against Fort Wayne on April 22. He was hospitalized and underwent a slew of medical tests before returning to the field. McCalvy noted that Peña's recovery timeline from ankle surgery remains unclear, though it is typically six to nine months.

item.title: [True Blue LA] Dodgers notes: Shohei Ohtani, Tyler Glasnow, first-round bye
item.dc:creator: Jacob Macofsky
item.description: Shohei Ohtani is back in the lineup and the Dodgers saved their best starting lineup for the final five games of the regular season. So far, the team has gone 2-18 with runners in scoring position while scoring just three runs over their two consecutive losses to the San Diego Padres. Thursday’s game in particular saw connect for two
item.content:encoded:
Shohei Ohtani is back in the lineup and the Dodgers saved their best starting lineup for the final five games of the regular season. So far, the team has gone 2-18 with runners in scoring position while scoring just three runs over their two consecutive losses to the San Diego Padres.
Ohtani was one of three Dodgers with an extra-base hit over their last two games, as the two-way superstar is 3-9 with a double, an RBI and a walk since returning. Thursday’s game in particular saw connect for two hits while smacking two deep fly balls that died on the center field warning track in their 4-2 loss, and the three weeks off have evidently helped him mitigate the unease he felt at the plate at the start of the month.
Andrew Friedman admitted the obvious, that the injuries to both his biceps and knee hampered his production at the plate, reports Jack Harris of the California Post, and he noted that he isn’t the most transparent when it comes to his physical health.
“There’s no question [the injuries] affected him,” Friedman said. “I think the fact that he feels as good as he does right now is certainly encouraging. Now it’s about making sure that holds.”
“He’s not always the best reporter of how he feels,” Friedman said. “Freddie [Freeman is] the same way. Clayton Kershaw. I’ve been around a lot of these guys that feel like their job is to be out there to help the team however they can, and sometimes will downplay some things that are bothering them.”
Despite Tyler Glasnow being dealt the loss in his final tune-up on Thursday, he impressed early on by flirting with a no-hitter through his first five innings while also racking up a season-high 11 strikeouts over 6 1/3 innings.
As the Dodgers begin to construct their ideal postseason pitching staff, Glasnow’s name is all but certain to be fixed into the rotation, and the right-hander stated that he’s in a good rhythm entering October while speaking to with the media postgame.
Last postseason, the Dodgers weren’t as fortunate to obtain a first-round bye, having to embark on a four-series gauntlet in their eventual success of becoming baseball’s first repeat champions in a quarter century.
With a much stronger regular season this time around, the Dodgers for the first time since 2024 will have that extra period of rest to prepare for their quest for a three-peat. The most significant factor for their first-round bye will be allowing players dealing with nagging issues to become as healthy as can be come October 3, per Sonja Chen of MLB.com.
“I think we all know why it’s important,” Freeman said earlier this week. “There’s a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here, a lot of aches and pains this year. It’s good to get those guys back on the field, get some ABs in them and then rest up and get some more ABs during the lives and whatever we do here in that week to get us ready for [NLDS Game 1].”

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

25 Sep 2026, 12:10 GMT+10

(Photo credit: William Purnell)
Miguel Vargas had two hits and two RBIs, Kyle Teel homered and David Sandlin delivered six strong innings as the visiting Chicago White Sox routed the Kansas City Royals 9-1 on Thursday to clinch an American League playoff berth.
Chicago is back in the postseason for the first time since 2021 after enduring three straight 100-loss seasons.
Fueled by an early barrage against Royals right-hander Randy Dobnak, the White Sox remained a game behind the AL Central-leading Cleveland Guardians. Chicago holds the head-to-head tiebreaker over Cleveland. Whichever one of those two teams fails to win the division will wind up as the third AL wild-card team.
Sandlin (3-2) yielded one run and five hits. Dobnak (3-5) allowed six runs (four earned) and six hits in 1 1/3 innings.
Guardians 1, Red Sox 0
Angel Martinez's second-inning home run was all visiting Cleveland needed for a win over Boston to clinch its third consecutive playoff berth.
Joey Cantillo (11-9) dominated for five shutout innings as the Guardians' bulk reliever, yielding one hit. Hunter Gaddis, Erik Sabrowski and Cade Smith allowed a combined one hit over the final three innings to help Cleveland win its seventh game in the last eight.
The playoff-bound Red Sox fell for the fourth time in five games despite getting five innings of one-run ball from Ranger Suarez (8-5).
Cubs 2, Marlins 1
Nico Hoerner ripped a go-ahead RBI single in the sixth and Matthew Boyd tossed seven strong innings, helping host Chicago clinch a playoff berth with a victory over Miami.
Chicago's Pete Crow-Armstrong walked to lead off the first inning and promptly stole second base to become the seventh player in major league history to record at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases in a single season.
Seiya Suzuki belted a solo homer in the fifth inning to highlight his two-hit performance for the Cubs, who salvaged the finale of their three-game series with Miami. Chicago sits in the second NL wild-card spot, one game behind San Diego.
Padres 4, Dodgers 2
Dustin Harris drove in the go-ahead run in the sixth inning as visiting San Diego beat Los Angeles to clinch a playoff spot for a franchise-record third consecutive season.
Yuki Matsui (4-1) earned the win with a scoreless inning, and Mason Miller gave up a run with two outs in the ninth before securing his 38th save. Ethan Salas and Fernando Tatis Jr. each had two hits and an RBI for the Padres.
Tyler Glasnow (5-2) fanned a season-high 11 but allowed three runs in 6 1/3 innings for the Dodgers, who secured a first-round playoff bye thanks to the Atlanta Braves' loss on Thursday. Shohei Ohtani went 2-for-5 with an RBI double.
Brewers 5, Phillies 1
Jake Bauers' RBI single in the eighth inning plated the go-ahead run for Milwaukee, which reached the 100-win mark for the first time in franchise history with a win at Philadelphia. When the Dodgers fell to the Padres later, the Brewers clinched the top record in the major leagues.
Bauers, who went 2-for-5, singled up the middle, allowing Jackson Chourio to score from second, giving the Brewers (100-59) a 2-1 lead and starting a three-run frame.
Philadelphia remains in an NL wild-card spot, but the Phillies could not drop their magic number to clinch from two. Phillies starter Andrew Painter threw six innings of one-run ball, fanning eight. Bryce Harper went 2-for-4 with an RBI.
Diamondbacks 12, Rockies 8
Gabriel Moreno and Nolan Arenado homered in a six-run first inning and surging Arizona beat Colorado in Denver to continue its drive for a wild-card berth.
James McCann also went deep for Arizona, which moved within two games of Philadelphia for the third and final NL playoff berth. Arizona finishes the regular season in San Diego while the Phillies host Tampa Bay this weekend.
Cole Carrigg homered among his four hits, Kyle Karros and Zac Veen also went deep and had two hits for Colorado, which finished with 17 hits.
Rangers 3, Mets 1
Kumar Rocker pitched five solid innings for Texas, which salvaged the finale of a three-game series against New York in Arlington, Texas.
Josh Jung (3-for-3) hit a two-run homer in the first and Corey Seager went deep in the sixth for the Rangers, who remain tied with Houston for first place in the American League West. Rocker (6-11) allowed one run on three hits. Jordan Montgomery recorded his first save of the season.
Mets starter Zac Thornton (5-6) yielded two runs on four hits over five innings. Brett Baty extended his on-base streak to 17 games.
Astros 7, Athletics 5
Rookie Lucas Spence hit his first three career homers and drove in five runs as Houston smacked five homers while defeating the Athletics in West Sacramento, Calif.
Isaac Paredes and Christian Walker added solo blasts for the Astros who remained tied for first in the AL West with the Rangers. Houston holds the tiebreaker, having gone 9-4 vs. Texas this year.
Houston reliever Miguel Ullola (2-0) fired three scoreless innings and Brayan Abreu worked 1 1/3 shutout innings for his ninth save. Zack Gelof hit two homers and Jeff McNeil drilled a three-run shot for the Athletics, who lost for the seventh time in nine games.
Yankees 6, Rays 4
Rookie George Lombard Jr. hit a tiebreaking two-run homer with two outs in the eighth inning as New York overcame a four-run deficit and earned a victory over visiting Tampa Bay.
New York ace Cam Schlittler allowed two runs (one earned) in three innings in a playoff tuneup, ending the season with a 1.95 ERA. Bradley Hanner (1-0) threw two scoreless innings for his first career victory.
Junior Caminero had a pair of RBI singles for the Rays. Ian Seymour allowed one hit in five scoreless innings. Steven Matz (5-6) served up Lombard's decisive homer.
Pirates 2, Cardinals 1
Spencer Horwitz's sacrifice fly in the eighth drove in the go-ahead run, and Paul Skenes concluded his season with a quality start as Pittsburgh wrapped up its home schedule with a victory over St. Louis.
Skenes tossed 6 1/3 innings, struck out eight, walked two and allowed one run on three hits. His final pitch completed a strikeout of Leo Bernal, giving him 200-plus for the second straight season. Luke Weaver (4-1) escaped an inherited eighth-inning jam before Mason Montgomery recorded his 17th save.
Alec Burleson homered for the Cardinals. St. Louis (77-82) is guaranteed to finish with back-to-back losing seasons for the first time since 1994-95.
Reds 7, Braves 6
A two-run homer by Hector Rodriguez, one of three long balls by Cincinnati, helped the visiting Reds beat Atlanta in the rubber game of a three-game series.
Rodriguez clubbed a 423-foot homer to right field against AJ Smith-Shawver (0-3) in the sixth inning to give the Reds the lead for good. Elly De La Cruz added his 30th homer and Carlos Jorge hit his first career homer. Cincinnati reliever Connor Phillips (2-0) pitched 1 1/3 scoreless innings.
Atlanta right-hander Tyler Mahle threw five innings and gave up five runs on six hits in his worst outing since being acquired from San Francisco at the trade deadline.
Angels 6, Mariners 4
Christian Moore doubled, singled and drove in three runs as Los Angeles won at Seattle.
Josh Lowe also had a single and a double and scored three times for the Angels. Los Angeles starter Grayson Rodriguez (5-8) gave up four runs on five hits over five innings. Ryan Watson pitched the ninth for his fourth save.
Julio Rodriguez homered for the Mariners, whose postseason hopes were dashed when the Rangers defeated the Mets earlier in the day. Bryan Woo (12-10) allowed five runs, four earned, on seven hits in 5 1/3 innings.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [The Sporting Tribune] Glasnow delivers strong final tune-up despite Dodgers loss
item.dc:creator: Fredo Cervantes
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Tyler Glasnow walked off the mound Thursday night having done almost everything the Dodgers could have asked of him. The result, however, belonged to the Padres. Glasnow carried a no-hit bid into the sixth inning and struck out 11 over 6⅓ innings in his final tune-up before the postseason, but the Padres broke through late and held on to beat the Dodgers, 4-2, in the final home game of the 2026 regular season at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium. The Dodgers finished the night 97-62,
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Tyler Glasnow walked off the mound Thursday night having done almost everything the Dodgers could have asked of him.
The result, however, belonged to the Padres.
Glasnow carried a no-hit bid into the sixth inning and struck out 11 over 6⅓ innings in his final tune-up before the postseason, but the Padres broke through late and held on to beat the Dodgers, 4-2, in the final home game of the 2026 regular season at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers finished the night 97-62, having already secured a first-round bye earlier Thursday. The Padres, meanwhile, clinched a postseason berth and will play in a Wild Card Series.
And with the postseason bracket beginning to take shape, there is a very real possibility these two teams could be back here in nine days.
For six innings, though, Glasnow looked every bit like a pitcher the Dodgers will want leading their rotation into October.
Ethan Salas broke up the no-hitter with a one-out single in the sixth. Salas eventually scored on a sacrifice fly, and two more singles helped the Padres add to its lead.
Glasnow entered the inning with the Dodgers still searching for their first run. He left it with the Padres ahead.
His final line was as sharp as the circumstances allowed: 6⅓ innings, three hits, three runs, all earned, two walks and 11 strikeouts on 91 pitches, 58 for strikes.
“I feel like I'm in a pretty good rhythm right now, so it's perfect time to bring it in to the postseason,” Glasnow said afterward.
The 11 strikeouts came on 79 pitches before he returned for the seventh, and the outing offered another encouraging sign for a Dodgers rotation preparing for the most important games of the season.
The Dodgers had opportunities against the Padres but repeatedly failed to capitalize, stranding seven runners through the middle innings.
Mookie Betts, meanwhile, continued to do what he has done all season: reach base.
Betts reached safely in all four plate appearances, going 3-for-4 with a double, two singles and a walk.
Shohei Ohtani also collected two hits, including an RBI double in the ninth inning that brought the Dodgers within two runs. Ohtani's late hit gave the Dodgers one final spark, but the Padres closed the door to finish off the regular-season home finale.
Dave Roberts said he has liked what he has seen from Ohtani over the past two games.
“The last 2 nights, he’s looked great,” Roberts said.
The Dodgers' final home game also provided another encouraging glimpse of Edwin Díaz.
Díaz worked a scoreless ninth, allowing no hits and striking out two on just 11 pitches. Since returning from the injured list, he has thrown four scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk while striking out eight.
Over his last four appearances, opponents are 1-for-13 with eight strikeouts.
Díaz said his slider is in its best shape right now, a development that comes at an important time as he tries to earn a spot on the Dodgers' postseason roster.
“I'm trying just to do my job. I'm just gonna wanna put zeros when they give me the ball,” Díaz said. “I'm ready to pitch every day. I just want them to keep trusting me and keep giving me the ball just to show them I'm ready to pitch in the postseason.”
Roberts called Thursday Díaz's best performance of his four appearances since returning.
“This has been the best of the four,” Roberts said.
There are only three regular-season games remaining, but the Dodgers have already accomplished one of their primary objectives. The first-round bye is secured. The home schedule is finished. Now comes the final push toward October.
The loss also did little to concern Roberts about the Dodgers' record against winning teams during the second half.
“I don’t think so, I don’t put stock into it,” Roberts said. “Once you get to the postseason, it’s a different game.”
That is the challenge waiting for the Dodgers.
Thursday was less about the standings than it was about getting their pieces in place. Glasnow looked in rhythm. Díaz continued to build momentum. Ohtani looked sharp at the plate. Betts reached base four times.
The Padres, meanwhile, celebrated a postseason berth in the visiting clubhouse.
There is still baseball to be played before October arrives. But with the Dodgers holding a bye and the Padres headed for the Wild Card round, Thursday's matchup may have offered a preview of a game that matters much more.
“We’re gonna have an exciting postseason, so just ride with us,” Roberts said.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

25 Sep 2026, 10:55 GMT+10

(Photo credit: William Liang)
Dustin Harris drove in the go-ahead run in the sixth inning as the visiting San Diego Padres made franchise history with a 4-2 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday to clinch a spot in the playoffs for a third consecutive season.
San Diego starter Nick Pivetta opened with 4 2/3 scoreless innings and four relievers finished off the victory as the Padres (89-70) celebrated a third straight playoff berth for the first time in franchise history. Yuki Matsui (4-1) earned the win with a scoreless inning and Mason Miller gave up a run with two outs in the ninth before securing his 38th save.
Austin Hays, Ethan Salas and Fernando Tatis Jr. added RBI singles in the seventh inning as San Diego won for the 15th time in its past 17 games. The Padres will open the playoffs in the wild-card round.
Tyler Glasnow took a no-hitter into the sixth inning for the Dodgers (97-62), who also secured their objective by clinching a spot in a National League Division Series matchup and the first-round bye that comes with it. Los Angeles sealed a top-two spot in the NL when the Cincinnati Reds defeated the Atlanta Braves earlier in the day.
Mookie Betts had three of the Dodgers' seven hits as he dropped to the No. 2 spot in the order for the first time in six games.
In his second game since returning from the injured list because of biceps discomfort, Shohei Ohtani moved back into the leadoff spot and went 2-for-5 with a two-out RBI double in the ninth. The Dodgers scored their first run in the eighth when Betts was awarded home plate on a balk by Adrian Morejon.
Pivetta kept his team in the game in giving up four hits with a walk and seven strikeouts while throwing 87 pitches in his final start of the regular season.
The Padres broke through against Glasnow in the sixth. Salas' one out single to center was San Diego's first hit of the game. Tatis followed with a single and Harris delivered a sacrifice fly to center for a 1-0 advantage.
San Diego chased Glasnow in the seventh with all three of the run-scoring hits in the inning coming against Justin Wrobleski. Glasnow was charged with three runs on three hits over his 6 1/3 innings with a season-high 11 strikeouts.
With a crowd of 53,027, the Dodgers passed the 4 million mark in attendance for the second consecutive season.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Dodgers clinch No. 2 seed and important playoff bye despite loss to Padres
item.dc:creator: Kevin Baxter
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The Dodgers clinched the National League’s No. 2 seed and a first-round playoff bye, gaining five crucial days to rest a battered roster before their Oct. 3 NLDS opener. - The Dodgers lose to the San Diego Padres 4-2 and drop the three-game series despite Tyler Glasnow carrying a no-hitter into the sixth inning. - The Padres clinched a postseason berth as the Dodgers prepare for their final regular-season series in San Francisco after drawing more
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers clinched the National League’s No. 2 seed and a first-round playoff bye, gaining five crucial days to rest a battered roster before their Oct. 3 NLDS opener.
- The Dodgers lose to the San Diego Padres 4-2 and drop the three-game series despite Tyler Glasnow carrying a no-hitter into the sixth inning.
- The Padres clinched a postseason berth as the Dodgers prepare for their final regular-season series in San Francisco after drawing more than 4 million fans to Dodger Stadium this season.
The Dodgers didn’t win Thursday. But they got something far more valuable before they even took the field for their 4-2 loss to the San Diego Padres.
With the Atlanta Braves’ loss to the Cincinnati Reds earlier in the day, the Dodgers clinched the second seed in the National League playoffs and the first-round bye that goes with it. That means the Dodgers will get five days off next week to prepare for their playoff opener, a godsend for a bruised and bloodied team that has stumbled to the finish of the regular season.
“I think we all know why it’s important,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said of the break. “There’s a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here, a lot of aches and pains this year.”
For the Padres (89-70), the victory was important because it clinched a wild-card berth and a franchise-record third consecutive trip to the postseason.
In addition to Freeman, who has been hobbled all month by a sore right knee, the Dodgers are rushing to get designated hitter Shohei Ohtani and closer Edwin Díaz healthy. Both had big games Thursday with Ohtani going two for five with a run batted in, the first time he’s had multiple hits or an RBI in more than a month. Díaz, meanwhile, pitched a perfect ninth, striking out two.
Other players also are getting healthy. Center fielder Andy Pages, who missed a month with a broken hand, returned to the lineup three days ago. Dalton Rushing, who is competing for a bench spot on the postseason roster, is expected to be activated off the injured list Friday. Left-hander Blake Snell, who came out of his last start nine days ago after just an inning, will make his final postseason tuneup Saturday.
All of them will benefit from some additional rest before their playoff opener, at Dodger Stadium, on Oct. 3.
And speaking of Dodger Stadium, the No. 2 playoff seed carries another important perk: the home-field advantage for the Division Series — and possibly the World Series, if the Dodgers make it that far. Home has certainly been an advantage for the Dodgers, who drew a sellout crowd of 53,027 Thursday, pushing the team’s total home attendance over 4 million for the second straight year.
“It’s more turning of the turnstiles than any venue in the world,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “The amazing thing is that it’s not just localized. It’s international. Everyone looks different at Dodger Stadium.
“It’s spectacular and our players certainly feed off of it.”
The Dodgers are one of five franchises in big-league history to draw more than 4 million fans in a season but just two others — the Toronto Blue Jays, from 1991-93, and the New York Yankees, in the final four years at old Yankee Stadium — did it in consecutive seasons.
And the Dodgers are the only team to do it since 2008. They also lead the majors in road attendance this season, having drawn 2.82 million, or 36,159 a game. For some fans, it’s hard to separate their support from the team’s success.
“A synergy exists between we the fans and the players,” said Charles Flores, an associate professor at Cal State L.A. and lifelong Dodgers fan who attended more than a dozen games this season. “One inspires the other.”
Russ Hoffman of Santa Clarita, a season-ticket holder for 40 years, agrees.
“The atmosphere created by drawing so many fans definitely contributes to their success,” he said. “Winning continuously drives the attendance and the current ownership has committed the assets to do that.”
That edge can be even bigger in the playoffs. The Dodgers lost just five of 16 postseason games at home — a .688 winning percentage — en route to World Series titles the last two years.
“During the playoffs, Dodger Stadium is a tough place to play because it’s 56,000 crazed fans yelling on every play,” said Stan Brooks, an award-winning film producer and longtime season-ticket holder. “The fans are so loud and the environment is so intense every night.”
The Dodgers (97-62) will finish the regular season with three games this weekend in San Francisco, where they will continue their preparation for the postseason.
In the final home game of the regular season Mookie Betts, dropped to second in the lineup with Ohtani’s return, went three for four with a walk, raising his average for September to .367, while Freeman had two hits for the third time in four games.
“I’m just encouraged with Shohei getting a couple hits, Mookie staying hot. That’s what it’s all about,” Freeman said. “Getting hot right now.
“That’s all we were looking forward to this last week is getting our guys back on the field.”
That didn’t add up to much offense Thursday, with the Dodgers stranding eight runners and going 0 for 8 with men in scoring position through eight innings. They avoided their first shutout of the season at home on Adrian Morejon’s balk in the eighth before Ohtani doubled in the second run with two outs in the ninth.
For the past 17 years, Chaz Perea and his four-person crew have been responsible for every bit of stadium landscaping that isn’t the field itself.
On the mound, Tyler Glasnow, who will be the Dodgers’ fourth starter in the postseason, was perfect through three innings. He walked Fernando Tatis Jr. on four pitches to start the fourth but didn’t allow another Padres batter to reach base until Ethan Salas singled with one out in the sixth.
That proved costly when Tatis singled on the next pitch, sending Salas to third, from where he scored on Dustin Harris’ sacrifice fly, putting the Padres ahead to stay.
Glasnow (5-2) got out of the inning by striking out Manny Machado, giving him a season-high 11 strikeouts and 21 in his last two starts. But San Diego then blew the game open in the seventh, chasing Glasnow and scoring three times off reliever Justin Wrobleski on run-scoring singles by Austin Hayes, Salas and Tatis.
Staff writer Maddie Lee contributed to this report.

item.title: [sandiegouniontribune.com] Padres beat Dodgers to clinch third straight postseason berth
item.dc:creator: Kevin Acee
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Finally, they are in. The Padres spent sizable portions of this season seemingly on the edge of collapse every few weeks before surging back into contention. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Finally, they are in.
The Padres spent sizable portions of this season seemingly on the edge of collapse every few weeks before surging back into contention.
So being no-hit for five innings and then suddenly building a sizable lead and then holding on in a frenzied finish to the game that clinched their playoff berth seemed about right.
The Padres got their first hit and their first run in the sixth inning and scored three more times in the seventh before turning the game over to the back end of their bullpen to preserve a 4-2 victory.
Their high-leverage relievers were the strength and the most consistent part of their team all season, so it was also fitting that Jason Adam, Adrian Morejón and Mason Miller strung together the final three innings to get the Padres into the playoffs for a third consecutive season.
It is the first time in team history the Padres have qualified for three consecutive postseasons and just the 10th time they will head to the playoffs in their 58 years of existence.
This was the second time in this three-year span that the Padres were spraying champagne in the visitors’ clubhouse at Dodger Stadium, the site of so many glum postgames over the years.
The Padres had reached base just once, on a walk, in five innings against Dodgers starter Tyler Glasnow.
Then, suddenly, they took a lead with the major contributions being a single by a rookie who joined them on Sept. 1 and a sacrifice fly by a journeyman who was called up on Aug. 24.
The Padres’ first hit of the night was Ethan Salas’ flare the other way and just over the left side of the infield with one out in the sixth inning.
Fernando Tatis Jr. followed with a single grounded through the right side that sent Salas to third base, and Dustin Harris then hit a fly ball to center field that put the Padres up 1-0.
Yuki Matsui, who had gotten the final out in the fifth inning, got the first two outs in the sixth before Jason Adam threw one pitch to get the third out.
A one-out double in the seventh inning by Jackson Merrill off Glasnow and a pinch-hit single by Austin Hays after lefty Justin Wrobleski entered the game extended the Padres’ lead, and two-out singles by Salas and Tatis extended it further.
Adam retired the first two batters in the seventh. Morejón got the final out that inning and allowed a run in the eighth. Miller’s 38th save was earned with a four-out ninth inning in which the Dodgers scored again.
After Tommy Edman reached base when he swung through a slider that bounced past Salas, Shohei Ohtani doubled Edman home before Mookie Betts grounded out.
Padres starter Nick Pivetta matched Glasnow where it mattered most — on the scoreboard — for as long as he could.
He was pulled after yielding a two-out single in the fifth inning, and Matsui surrendered a single to Freddie Freeman before striking out Teoscar Hernández.
The Dodgers found out before the game that they had clinched a first-round bye in the playoffs, so they are essentially playing out the season to stay in shape.
Exactly three years after the Padres clinched a playoff berth with a victory at Dodger Stadium, they were playing on Thursday for the right to continue playing.
They are now striving over the next three days for the right to host their best-of-three National League Wild Card Series.
They are in position to do so, a game ahead of the Cubs, who also clinched a playoff berth Thursday. Because the Cubs won the series between the teams, the Padres have to finish a game ahead of the Cubs in the standings in order to remain the No.4 seed.
